title: A UNC path's "drive" isn't a drive letter at all — it's the whole \\server\share
assumption: splitdrive on a Windows path always returns either nothing or a single letter plus a colon.

input.description: A network path (a mapped file server, a backup target) handled by code that was only ever tested against local drive-letter paths.

what_goes_wrong: Code that assumes the 'drive' component is either empty or exactly two characters ("C:") mishandles a UNC path, truncating or misinterpreting the server/share portion that ntpath actually bundles into the drive.
why: ntpath.splitdrive special-cases UNC syntax: for a path starting with two separators followed by a server and share name, it returns the ENTIRE \\server\share prefix as the 'drive', not just a letter and colon, because that whole prefix has to stay together to resolve the rest of the path. Node's path.win32.parse does the analogous thing, putting the full \\server\share\ into `root`. A function written only against "C:" paths, and assuming a fixed two-character drive length, breaks silently on the far longer UNC form.
fix: Use the library's own splitdrive/parse output rather than assuming a fixed-width drive prefix, and test path-handling code against UNC paths explicitly, not just local drive letters.

sources.title: Microsoft Learn: Naming Files, Paths, and Namespaces (UNC paths)

test_cases.note: If your code assumes a drive component is always empty or exactly 'C:', test it against a UNC path like this one.
